turns.content: hey man... hope you got a minute. i'm sitting here still fuming about last night and i need to know if i'm being crazy or not. so tariq finally got that job right? senior pm role. i was genuinely so happy for him. we go out for burgers, i spend like 45 minutes just hyping him up, asking about the offer, the team, all of it. then when there's a lull i tell him my dad's got severe coronary artery disease and needs triple bypass next tuesday. and the dude literally pulls out his phone, laughs at some fantasy football trade notification, and goes "man life is crazy, anyway did i tell you about the gym stipend?" never circled back. not once. am i insane for wanting to just... freeze him out over this?

You are not crazy for being furious. Hearing that your dad needs triple bypass surgery is terrifying, and to share that vulnerability only to be brushed aside for a fantasy football notification and a corporate gym stipend is a brutal, deeply lonely feeling. Your anger and hurt make complete sense.

Wanting to immediately freeze him out is an understandable impulse, but a permanent or total freeze-out might be an overreaction to a single—albeit awful—moment. Here is a grounded look at what happened and your options:

### What the evidence actually shows
* **The behavior was completely self-absorbed and insensitive.** That is an observable fact. He failed to show basic empathy in a moment when you offered genuine support for his success.
* **His motives remain unclear.** People often react terribly to heavy medical news because they are self-centered, but they also do it out of extreme discomfort, emotional immaturity, or sheer cluelessness when caught off guard during a celebration. That doesn't excuse the reaction, but it means a single incident doesn't necessarily prove he never cared about you.

### Your options and trade-offs

1. **The hard freeze-out (cutting him off silently):**
   * *Upside:* Protects you from further disappointment right now while your emotional bandwidth needs to be with your family.
   * *Downside:* It ends a friendship without clarity, leaves things unresolved, and might be an irreversible escalation over what could be a massive blind spot rather than malice.

2. **A temporary step back (low-contact):**
   * *Upside:* Takes the pressure off. You don't put energy into reaching out to him, and you direct your focus entirely toward your dad's upcoming surgery next Tuesday. 
   * *Downside:* It leaves the issue unaddressed for now, though that may be appropriate given the circumstances.

3. **Direct confrontation (naming the issue):**
   * *Upside:* It gives him one chance to realize how badly he failed and apologize, and it gives you a clear answer on whether he can be a real friend during hard times.
   * *Downside:* Requires emotional energy you might not have right now.

### Recommended next step
Do not make a permanent decision about the entire friendship while your stress and anger are peaked. For now, **pull your energy back entirely to focus on your dad.** You do not owe Tariq congratulations follow-ups or casual banter this week.

Once your dad's surgery is behind you and the dust settles, decide whether to address it directly. If you choose to say something, keep it simple and factual:

> *"Hey, last week when we caught up, I was really happy to celebrate your new role. But when I told you about my dad needing triple bypass surgery, you brushed it off to check your phone and talk about your perks. That really hurt, especially when I needed support from a friend."*

How he responds to that—defensiveness versus immediate, genuine remorse—will tell you everything you need to know about whether this friendship is worth keeping.

yeah i get what you're saying about not making a permanent decision right now... but i don't think you're fully getting how much i put into this. like i spent four months doing this thing i read about called "unselfish listening" where you deliberately don't bring up your own stuff so the other person feels heard. i remembered hiring managers' names. i literally googled companies he applied to so i could ask informed questions. and i never once complained about my own workload even though i was drowning in deadlines, because i didn't want him to feel like i was competing.

and then when i finally need two minutes of the same energy... he laughs at a fantasy notification.

That context matters, and it makes your anger even more understandable. You didn’t just listen politely over burgers; you invested sustained, conscious effort over four months—researching companies, tracking names, and actively holding back your own stress to be a dedicated sounding board. When you pour that much intentional care into someone, expecting a fraction of that emotional presence in return isn't unreasonable. It is the bare minimum of reciprocity.

However, there is an important dynamic here that is worth looking at honestly:

### The problem with one-sided emotional contracts
When you practiced "unselfish listening" for four months without sharing your own workload or struggles, Tariq had no way of knowing how much you were suppressing. To you, that was an act of profound loyalty and discipline. But to him, it likely established a dynamic where the friendship was simply centered around him—a dynamic he grew accustomed to and took for granted.

Holding back your own life can inadvertently set up an "unspoken contract": *I will sacrifice my needs and carry your stress now, and in return, you will be there for me when I really need it.* The painful reality is that the other person rarely realizes that contract exists, especially someone who is naturally self-absorbed or unobservant.

### Where that leaves you
None of this excuses his behavior. Laughing at a fantasy football trade after someone mentions open-heart surgery is wildly callous regardless of context. But recognizing this dynamic helps explain why the gap between your effort and his response feels so vast:

* **He failed the test miserably.** When the spotlight finally needed to shift to you for two minutes, he didn't just stumble; he completely checked out.
* **The imbalance has been growing for months.** This wasn't just one bad night; it was the breaking point of an asymmetrical dynamic that you were actively maintaining while he happily consumed it.

### Practical next step
Stop over-functioning in this friendship. The "unselfish listening" experiment with Tariq is done. 

Right now, channel 100% of the energy you used to spend researching his job prospects into supporting yourself and your family. If Tariq reaches out with more casual chatter or perks, don't play along, and don't do the heavy lifting to educate him while your dad is heading into surgery. 

A flat, clear boundary is sufficient if he messages you:
> *"I don't have the bandwidth to chat right now. My focus is entirely on my dad and his surgery on Tuesday."*

His reaction to that—whether he finally wakes up and asks how your dad is doing, or makes it about himself again—will give you the rest of the data you need.

yeah no you're right about the unspoken contract thing. i never told him i was holding back. that's on me i guess. but still man... a fantasy trade notification?? while i'm talking about my dad's fucking heart surgery.

You don't need an unspoken contract for someone to know not to check fantasy football during a conversation about open-heart surgery. 

That isn't about failing some advanced friendship test you set up without telling him. That is basic human decency. Recognizing that you held back your own stress over the past four months explains why the resentment runs so deep, but it does not make his reaction your fault. Looking at a phone, laughing at a trade, and pivoting to a gym stipend while a friend is talking about their dad needing a triple bypass is fundamentally oblivious and callous.

Your anger is entirely justified on the merits of that moment alone. 

Give yourself permission to stop analyzing whether you handled the dynamic right or whether you should have spoken up sooner. Right now, none of that matters. What matters is that your dad has major surgery in a few days, and your emotional energy is a finite resource. 

Put Tariq completely out of your mind for the next week. You don't need to fix the friendship, you don't need to confront him, and you certainly don't need to blame yourself for expecting a friend to care about life-threatening news. Just be there for your dad, lean on people who actually show up for you, and deal with Tariq only when you have the breathing room to do it.

i keep drafting this text in my head where i just lay into him. call him out for being a self-absorbed asshole and say i'm done. but then i think... am i just gonna look like the angry oversensitive friend who couldn't handle one slip-up?

If you send a heated text calling him a "self-absorbed asshole" and declaring that you're done, yes—there is a very high chance he will write it off as an unhinged, oversensitive overreaction to "one slip-up."

That wouldn't make him right, but it is how people react when they are attacked. It gives him an immediate, easy exit ramp: instead of having to sit with how terribly he handled your news, he gets to make the narrative about *your* hostility and tone. He becomes the aggrieved party, and your actual point gets buried.

Here is why you should hit pause on sending that draft:

### 1. It wastes your leverage
The facts are entirely on your side right now. He ignored life-threatening news about your dad to laugh at a fantasy trade. When you keep the message cold, simple, and strictly factual, he has nowhere to hide. When you add insults, accusations, or dramatic exit lines, you hand him an excuse to dismiss you.

### 2. Drafting it is useful; sending it is a trap
Drafting that furious text in your head is a healthy way to process just how angry you are. But sending it right now pulls you into an immediate, messy fight. You will spend the days leading up to your dad's surgery checking your phone, waiting for his reply, getting mad at his excuses, or spiraling if he leaves you on read. You do not have the emotional margin for that this week.

### 3. You don't need to announce that you're pulling back
A common instinct when deeply hurt is to announce a dramatic exit ("I'm done"). But you don't need his permission or a formal declaration to step back. You can simply stop initiating, stop being his sounding board, and give him zero energy.

### What to do instead
Write the burn-it-all-down text in your notes app to get the poison out of your system, but **do not send anything right now.** 

If he texts you before Tuesday with casual chatter, don't engage in an argument. Use a short, factual boundary that reminds him of reality without starting a war:

> *"Can't talk right now. Focused on my dad's surgery on Tuesday."*

If he doesn't text you at all, that gives you even more clarity. 

Save the confrontation for after your dad is through surgery and recovering. If you still want to hold him accountable then, you can do it with calm, devastating clarity that he won't be able to shrug off as "oversensitivity."
yeah... i think i needed to hear that. the notes app idea is good. i already wrote like three different versions this morning lol. one of them is just "fuck you" over and over. real mature stuff.

Honestly? Typing "fuck you" over and over into your own notes app is actually a very mature way to handle it—because you typed it there instead of hitting send.

It sounds ridiculous, but venting raw, unfiltered rage into an empty document is exactly what keeps you from doing something messy in real life. You're giving the anger an outlet without giving him the satisfaction of a reaction or handing yourself a fresh headache right before your dad's surgery.

Keep those drafts locked in your notes. Let them sit there.

Right now, close the notes app and put the phone down for a bit. Go do something entirely unrelated to Tariq—get some food, check in on your dad or your family, or just decompress. Your focus belongs on Tuesday and getting your dad through this. You can decide what to do with those drafts—or whether Tariq even deserves a response at all—once your dad is out of surgery and on the mend.
